description.value: The study examined how reward-related contextual feedback is learned and integrated with sensory, motor, and cognitive control systems during perceptual motion decisions.

spans.text: In the present study, we examined how bias is developed in perceptual decision-making and once developed how it influences the perceptual decision-making process in the brain.

design.value: A model-based fMRI study using a motion discrimination task with two reward contexts, trial-wise reward feedback, reinforcement-learning models, parametric fMRI analyses, and psychophysiological interaction analyses.

spans.text: We addressed these questions using model-based neuroimaging in a motion discrimination paradigm where contextual cues suggested which one of two options would receive higher rewards on each trial.

During fMRI acquisition, participants performed a motion discrimination task (Newsome et al., ; Britten et al., ; Shadlen and Newsome, ) with pre-trial cues signaling one of two different reward contexts.

model_settings.value: Two Q-learning models were specified: a context-dependent model and a context-free model; a logit function generated binary choice probabilities from subjective value differences and motion stimulus strength.

spans.text: Two Q-learning models (Watkins and Dayan, ) were separately specified such that the reward prediction error (RPE) was used to update action value differently.

model_settings.value: The first-level model included parametric modulated regressors for absolute coherence, trial-wise bias, and reward prediction error, plus nuisance regressors for trial-evoked activity, reaction time, motion parameters, FD, DVARS, and scrubbed time points.

spans.text: The parametric modulated regressors included (1) the absolute value of the coherence level (duration between the onset and offset of the stimulus), (2) the trial-wise amount of bias (duration between trial onset and stimulus offset), and (3) the reward prediction error derived from both learning models (duration between the onset and offset of the reward feedback).

Nuisance regressors in the model were (1) a boxcar regressor encoding trial-evoked activity (duration between the onset of the context and the next ITI), (2) a boxcar regressor between the stimulus onset and the time when a key press was detected to control the reaction time (RT), and (3) a confound file including all the motion correction parameters
